summary:
Kalmykia, an autonomous republic of the Russian Federation, is assessed under the UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression for Russia (version 2.0, June 2025). That note records that consensual same-sex activity is not criminalised in Russia, while same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned and the constitution offers no specific legal protections for LGBT+ people. The note contains no Kalmykia-specific information; the national framework sets the standard for what a transgender visitor to the republic should expect.

Legal gender recognition is prohibited outright. The law signed by President Vladimir Putin in 2023 bans gender reassignment surgery and any change of gender marker on official documents, voids a marriage concluded by a trans person with someone of their same birth sex, and removes the right to adopt from people diagnosed with gender dysphoria. Trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned the same year. A 2024 law additionally bars adoption of Russian children by citizens or permanent residents of countries that permit gender transitions.

Public expression is constrained by the propaganda statutes, which since their December 2022 expansion reach material promoting "non-traditional" sexual relationships, making minors interested in gender transition, or giving minors a "desire to change their sex"; the provisions cover speech that justifies gender transition. Penalties reach fines of up to 400,000 rubles (about £3,600) or up to 15 days' detention, and repeated offences risk criminal prosecution. The UK Home Office note records that at least 139 individuals were affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement between 2022 and 2024. Human Rights Watch counted 257 "gay propaganda" penalties imposed in 2023-24 against 22 in 2021-22.

Since the Supreme Court's November 2023 designation of an "international LGBT movement" as extremist, charges have been brought for displaying the rainbow flag or its colours. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions as of 30 June 2025, with sentences of up to 12 years in prison, for participation in that movement or display of its symbols. The same organisation documented 81 people found guilty in 98 administrative cases under article 20.3 since January 2024 for displaying banned symbols, mostly on social media. Within 48 hours of the designation, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars in Moscow, and between March and May 2026 nine LGBTQ organisations were outlawed as extremist.

Russia provides no anti-discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, does not designate hate crimes as such, does not treat gender-identity or sexual-orientation motivation as an aggravating factor, and does not officially record hate crimes against the LGBTQ community. Coercive conversion practice against trans people is documented: a transgender woman was lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a centre near Novosibirsk and held for nine months, forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour.

Entry and onward protection carry explicit warnings. The US State Department advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, with language relevant to LGBT travellers. The UK Home Office note affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, the assessment standard for UK asylum claims. Reporting published in June 2024 profiles transgender Russians caught between leaving and staying, and analysis from August 2024 describes the court-driven purge and mass emigration of LGBT Russians; for many, emigration has become the only remaining means of living openly.
tangentialFactors:
Human Rights Watch's figures are national enforcement totals rather than Kalmykia-specific counts, and the UK Home Office note likewise states that it contains no division-specific information beyond the Russian national framework. Kalmykia is treated here as one data point within a nationwide pattern of enforcement, which intensified sharply after the Supreme Court's November 2023 extremist designation.

The trajectory of enforcement is measurable. More than 180 cases were brought under the propaganda provisions in 2023 alone, exceeding the total for 2013 to 2022 combined and producing roughly 26 million rubles in fines; cases under these statutes have increased eighteenfold over the past decade, and fines brought over 60 million rubles (about $765,300) into the state budget in the two years to mid-2025. Charges under the extremist designation cover both the administrative and criminal codes, so conduct that draws an administrative penalty in one instance can draw a prison sentence in another.

The autonomous republic of Chechnya, cited in the UK Home Office note as part of the territory where LGBT+ people form a particular social group, is the best-known regional outlier for organised persecution; Kalmykia has no comparable documented record, but neither is there evidence of any local protection regime differing from the national one. A man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel business was found dead in a pretrial detention facility in December 2024, an indicator of risk inside custody.

Loss of family-law standing extends beyond the visitor: marriage voiding, the adoption bar and the 2024 restriction on intercountry adoption to residents of countries permitting gender transitions narrow the legal position of trans people and of foreign partners alike.
localsOnly:
Residents of Kalmykia live under the same prohibitions as visitors, with the added exposure of a fixed address. Gender marker change and gender-affirming surgery are unavailable anywhere in Russia, and trans-specific healthcare has been effectively banned since 2023, leaving diagnosis of gender dysphoria itself as a status that strips adoption rights.

Ordinary self-expression carries penalties. Fines reach 400,000 rubles and 15 days' detention for propaganda offences, repeat offences escalate to criminal prosecution, and displaying the rainbow flag or its colours since November 2023 has produced extremism charges carrying sentences of up to 12 years. Administrative liability under article 20.3 for banned symbols has been applied overwhelmingly to social-media posts.

The organisations that once offered support have been dissolved or outlawed: nine LGBTQ organisations, among them the Russian LGBT Network, Coming Out and Centre T, were designated extremist between March and May 2026, following the November 2023 designation of the "international LGBT movement" itself. Membership, funding or display of associated symbols can now be framed as extremist participation.

There is no statutory protection against dismissal, refusal of service or housing discrimination on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation, no hate-crime designation, no aggravating factor for anti-trans or anti-LGB motivation, and no official recording of such hate crimes. Coercive confinement by relatives at faith-based conversion centres has been documented, with the November 2021 Novosibirsk-region case showing that police intervention was possible only when the detainee obtained a phone.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Kalmykia-specific enforcement data, detention records or local court outcomes are present in the source inventory; the figures cited for propaganda penalties, administrative cases and extremism convictions are national totals for the Russian Federation. Whether Kalmykia's enforcement matches or diverges from the national rate is not sourced.

The inventory contains no information on availability of HIV care, competent medical treatment in custody, local documentation procedures for foreign trans visitors, or the practical handling of gender-marker mismatch at Russian border crossings for persons entering Kalmykia; these remain unresolved rather than confirmed absent.

The claimed penalty ceiling for propaganda offences (400,000 rubles or 15 days' detention) is drawn from the UK Home Office note as rendered in the inventory; the interaction of that administrative ceiling with criminal liability for repeat offences is stated qualitatively and the exact recidivism thresholds are not sourced here.

Whether Kalmykia-level authorities have pursued extremism charges in addition to the national cases counted by Human Rights Watch is not stated in the sources.
